questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signed link guarantees
questions.learningObjective: State what a signed link guarantees and what it leaves open.
questions.stem: An architect's brief proposes a signed link between two zones and claims it makes the traffic safe to trust. What does the signature actually guarantee?

options.text: The traffic came from a key holder and was unaltered in transit, but nothing is said about the payload itself.
The traffic is confidential and authentic, so the receiving zone can trust whatever the sending zone sends.
options.misconception: assumes signing also provides confidentiality of the payload

options.text: The traffic is authentic and safe to execute, so the receiving zone need not inspect the payload before running.
options.misconception: assumes authenticity makes the payload safe to execute

options.text: The traffic is authentic and policy-permitted, so signature checking replaces the receiving zone's access rules.
options.misconception: assumes a valid signature substitutes for authorisation policy

questions.explanation: A signature proves origin and integrity: the payload came from the key holder and was not changed. It gives neither confidentiality nor a judgement about content, so the receiver still applies its own rules.
questions.hint: Ask what a signature attests to, not what it hides.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What each layer of an envelope encrypts
questions.learningObjective: Describe what each layer of an envelope scheme protects.
questions.stem: Describe what an envelope encryption scheme protects at each layer, and why the layers are not interchangeable.

answer.exemplar: The outer layer wraps the data key under a key the recipient can unwrap, so the wrapped key and the ciphertext reveal nothing without the recipient's key. The inner layer encrypts the data itself under that data key, so each item can be encrypted and released separately under a key that never travels with the payload. The layers are not interchangeable because the outer layer determines who may open the item at all, while the inner layer determines what each opened item contains, and only the inner layer can be scoped narrowly per item.

questions.explanation: The outer layer protects the data key and the whole item, while the inner layer protects the payload. Only the inner layer can be scoped per item, so the layers answer different questions.
questions.hint: Ask what each layer actually encrypts.

options.misconception: assumes an explicit allow list with a default deny at the end

questions.topic: Rule order decides which restriction applies
questions.learningObjective: Identify what determines which overlapping rule governs.
questions.stem: An architect's brief lists two restrictions on the same path and asks which one governs. What determines the answer?

options.text: The stricter rule governs, because the engine merges both restrictions and applies the tighter outcome.
options.misconception: assumes matching rules are merged rather than resolved in order

options.text: The rule written most recently governs, because the newest definition overrides the older one.
options.misconception: assumes the most recently written rule wins over earlier ones

options.text: The order of the rules governs, because the first rule that matches a request decides, so earlier rules take precedence.
Neither governs alone, because a request matching both is refused until the rules are reconciled.
options.misconception: assumes overlapping rules block by default instead of being resolved

questions.explanation: Rule engines resolve a request by taking the first matching rule, so position in the list decides the outcome when two restrictions overlap. Nothing merges the two rules and nothing fails closed by default.
questions.hint: Ask which matching rule is evaluated first.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signed link guarantees
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a signed link proves and what the receiver must still do.
questions.stem: Explain what a signed link guarantees, what it does not, and what a receiver must still do with the payload.

answer.exemplar: A valid signature establishes that the payload was produced by the holder of the signing key and was not modified on the way, so the receiver can attribute the message and detect tampering. It establishes nothing about the content's safety, its confidentiality, or whether the sender was entitled to send it, and the transport may be readable to anyone on the path. The receiver must therefore validate the signature itself, because an unverified signature proves nothing, and must still apply its own authorisation and inspection to the payload before acting on it.

questions.explanation: The signature attests to origin and integrity only. The receiver must verify it rather than assume it, and it still has to authorise the sender and inspect the content, since neither is implied.
questions.hint: Ask what the receiver still has to decide.

options.text: The outer layer encrypts each object directly, so no per-object data key is required at all.

options.text: The inner layer encrypts each object, and the single-decrypt property means objects need no separate keys.
options.misconception: misreads a per-request property as a per-object design change

options.text: The inner layer encrypts each object under its own data key, and one unwrap suffices since no request needs two.

questions.explanation: The per-object data key belongs to the inner layer, since that is what encrypts the object, while the outer layer only wraps those data keys. One object per request means a single unwrap per request is enough.
questions.hint: Ask which layer touches the object itself.

questions.topic: Choosing between a customer-managed and a provider-managed key
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the two key models and the trade each represents.
questions.stem: Explain the difference between a customer-managed key and a provider-managed key, and state which one a team should pick when it must control key material itself.

answer.exemplar: With a provider-managed key the platform creates, stores and rotates the key material, so the team never holds it and gets rotation and lifecycle handling without effort. With a customer-managed key the team supplies the key material and keeps control of it, including the right to revoke it, while taking on the duties of securing, rotating and auditing it. A team that must control the key material itself can only have the customer-managed option, but should budget for the rotation and evidence work that comes with it.

questions.explanation: The provider-managed option keeps key material away from the team and handles lifecycle; the customer-managed option keeps control of the material but transfers the duties of securing, rotating and evidencing it.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the key material in each case.

questions.stem: Propose the correction for a network policy whose trailing rule allows everything, and explain why the current text misleads a reviewer.

answer.exemplar: Make the default deny and express the permitted paths as explicit allows, or keep the structure but add deny rules for every path that must never be reachable, so unmatched traffic is refused rather than admitted. The current text misleads because a reader skims the named rules and sees precise port and destination restrictions, which suggests a tight policy. The trailing rule reverses that impression, and since the list contains no deny rules there is nothing to catch the flows that match nothing at all.

questions.explanation: The trailing allow-all rule overrides the impression created by named restrictions, and without deny rules nothing catches unmatched flows. Making the default deny, or adding explicit denies, restricts traffic.
questions.hint: Ask what the last rule does with anything unnamed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The audit a secrets manager provides
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a secret store's audit trail can and cannot show.
questions.stem: Explain what the audit trail of a managed secret store can and cannot tell an investigator about a leaked credential.

answer.exemplar: The store's records can show which principal read which secret at what time and from where, and a rotation history can show which version was live during a window. That supports the question of who could have obtained a value and when. They cannot show whether the value was copied, whether it was used successfully elsewhere, or whether a human simply read it for legitimate work, because the store records access rather than the fate of the secret afterwards.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What each layer of an envelope encrypts
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an envelope scheme wraps the data key.
questions.stem: Explain why an envelope scheme wraps the data key rather than encrypting every object under one long-term key.

answer.exemplar: Encrypting every object directly under the recipient's long-term key means every decryption needs that key, so releasing one object requires decrypting all of them, and a compromise of the key exposes the entire store at once. Wrapping a separate data key per object means the recipient unwraps a key for one item, decrypts that item and nothing else, and revoking one wrapped key affects only that item. The long-term key is then only ever used to unwrap, which is a far smaller and more frequent operation to protect.

questions.explanation: One long-term key over many objects means no item can be released alone and one compromise exposes everything. A per-item wrapped data key allows individual release and revocation, the point of the envelope.
questions.hint: Ask what one key compromise would expose.

answer.exemplar: The audit trail exists so that the team can answer who read which secret, when, and from where, and it turns credential handling from an assumption into a record that can be examined. answer.exemplar: A signature answers two questions: did this payload come from the holder of the key, and has it been altered on the way. It says nothing about who else read it. Nothing is achieved yet, because a single remaining environment variable defeats the whole pattern.
options.misconception: dismisses progress because one exception remains

options.text: The store now records every access, because the environment variable is fetched through the same client.
options.misconception: assumes a local copy is fetched through the store client

questions.explanation: The pattern holds for the services that fetch from the store, and those fetches are recorded. The service reading an environment variable holds a copy the store never sees, so it escapes the trail.
questions.hint: Ask where that remaining copy actually lives.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A network policy whose unmatched traffic is allowed
questions.learningObjective: State what a policy with a trailing allow rule actually restricts.
questions.stem: First stage: a network policy allows traffic to the internal service on port 8080 and then allows all remaining traffic. Second stage: the reviewer asks what the policy actually restricts.

options.text: Only traffic on port 8080, because the allow rule names the traffic it permits.
options.misconception: assumes naming a permitted port excludes every other port

options.text: Almost nothing, because the trailing allow-all admits every flow the port rule did not cover.
Traffic to the internal service, because the first rule applies to that destination only.
options.misconception: ignores the trailing allow-all and treats the first rule as exclusive

options.text: Everything except traffic to the internal service, which the port rule implicitly protects.
options.misconception: inverts the effect of the named rule

questions.explanation: The trailing allow-all admits every flow the port rule did not match, so the policy's restriction is limited to what a deny rule would add. Naming a permitted port does not exclude the others.
questions.hint: Ask what the trailing rule does with other ports.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The access pattern a jump host constrains
questions.learningObjective: State the access pattern a jump host imposes.
questions.stem: A brief describes a jump host that operators use to reach production. Which statement describes the resulting access pattern most precisely?

options.text: Every session to production terminates on one host, so the estate exposes a single, recordable entry point.
Every session to production is separately approved by the host, so no session runs without a decision.
options.misconception: assumes the host makes a per-session authorisation decision

options.text: Every operator shares one account on the host, so the estate loses per-operator accountability.
options.misconception: assumes a choke point collapses operator identities

options.text: Operators reach production directly and the host only records what it observes afterwards.
options.misconception: describes the host as an observer rather than the route

questions.explanation: The jump host is where the session terminates, so production presents one entry point that can be recorded, limited and reviewed. It does not make per-session decisions and does not merge identities.
questions.hint: Ask where the session physically ends.

questions.topic: The access pattern a jump host constrains
questions.learningObjective: Count the accounts that can reach at least one tier.
questions.stem: A jump host serves 3 tiers: 4 administrators who may reach production, 12 operators who may reach staging, and 30 read-only accounts that reach no tier. How many accounts can reach at least one tier?
questions.explanation: The administrators and operators can reach a tier, and the read-only accounts cannot, so 4 plus 12 gives 16 accounts with access. The 30 read-only accounts contribute none to the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What each layer of an envelope encrypts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what each envelope layer protects and why one is not enough.
questions.stem: Explain what the inner and outer layers of an envelope scheme each protect, and why the outer layer alone is not enough.

answer.exemplar: The inner layer encrypts the content under a data key that belongs to that one item, so the item is protected and can be released on its own. The outer layer wraps that data key under a key the recipient holds, so the wrapped key itself reveals nothing to anyone else. The outer layer cannot replace the inner because it never touches the content, and without the inner layer the content would sit in the clear with only its key wrapped.

questions.explanation: The inner layer protects the content under a per-item data key; the outer layer protects that data key under the recipient's key. The outer layer alone protects no content, since it never touches what is stored.
questions.hint: Ask which layer touches the content itself.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Choosing between a customer-managed and a provider-managed key
questions.learningObjective: Count the archives covered by a provider-managed key.
questions.stem: An architect records that a customer-managed key covers 40 of 65 archives in the estate and a provider-managed key covers the remainder. How many archives does the provider-managed key cover?

options.text: Twenty-five archives, since 65 minus 40 leaves the remainder for the provider-managed key.
Forty archives, since the provider-managed key must match the customer-managed coverage.
options.misconception: assumes the two models must cover equal numbers

options.text: Sixty-five archives, because a provider-managed key applies to the whole estate at once.
options.misconception: misses that the provider-managed key covers only the remainder

options.text: Twenty archives, because the two key models overlap on part of the estate.
options.misconception: invents an overlap the scenario does not describe

questions.explanation: The customer-managed key covers 40 of the 65 archives, so the remaining 25 fall to the provider-managed key. Nothing in the scenario suggests the two models overlap or must match.
questions.hint: Take the estate total minus the customer-managed count.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a signed link guarantees
questions.learningObjective: Judge what a signed link establishes and what it leaves exposed.

stimulus.body: A brief proposes signing the traffic between two zones so that the receiving side can attribute every request to the sending side. A second line of the brief records that the two zones are connected over a shared carrier path, and the receiving zone currently stores the payloads in a shared queue that several internal teams can read.

questions.stem: According to the brief, what does signing give the receiving zone, and what exposure does the brief leave open?

options.text: Signing protects the payloads from internal teams, because a signed payload can only be read by its verifier.
options.misconception: assumes signing restricts who may read the payload

options.text: Signing ensures only the sending side can read the payloads, since only it holds the signing key.
options.misconception: assumes the signing key is also a decryption key

options.text: Signing removes the need for access controls on the queue, because attribution is enough to keep it private.
options.misconception: assumes attribution is a substitute for access control on storage

options.text: Signing attributes each request to the sending side, but the shared queue still exposes the payloads to internal teams.

questions.explanation: A signature attributes the payload to the holder of the key; it does not restrict who may read what has been stored. The shared queue therefore still exposes the payloads to the internal teams that read it.
questions.hint: Ask whether signing limits readers or only names the sender.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Choosing between a customer-managed and a provider-managed key
questions.learningObjective: Assess what a mixed key model achieves and what it costs.
questions.stem: First stage: an architect chooses a customer-managed key for the estate's most sensitive archives and a provider-managed key for the remainder. Second stage: the reviewer asks what the split actually achieves.

options.text: It gives the sensitive archives a stronger key, since customer-managed keys are always cryptographically stronger.
options.misconception: confuses who controls a key with how strong it is

options.text: It removes the need for any key review, because the split divides the responsibility between two services.
options.misconception: assumes splitting responsibility removes the need for review

options.text: It lets the team stop rotating keys entirely, because the provider-managed half is handled automatically.
options.misconception: assumes one half being automatic removes work for the other half

options.text: It keeps control of sensitive material and outsources the rest, at the cost of running two models.

questions.explanation: The split lets the team keep control of the material where it matters most and outsource lifecycle work elsewhere. It does not change key strength, and it leaves two models to review rather than one.
questions.hint: Ask what the team gains and what it now operates.
